en: The Hymn of Description from the Hair of Śiva’s Head to His Feet.

May the matted locks of Śiva grant you welfare—locks that bestow upon the King’s head a golden hue, like the tall, tawny stalks of ripe red rice-creepers reaching to the far banks of the celestial river;

which serve as ropes for the rescue of the wretched people fallen into the pit of irresistible calamity; and which, with their flames of fire burning the terrible forest of worldly existence, create the illusion of silver steps shining on the path to liberation, appearing like the distinct lines marking the triple victory over the ancient cities of Indra’s enemies.

May the triple mark (*tripuṇḍra*) of the Lord of Mṛḍānī protect you—mark which is free from artifice, lofty, resembling the rising Gaṅgā on the slopes of the sunless mountain of the forehead, and white with the ash of Rudra.

May the eye of Umā, situated on her forehead, grant you the fulfillment of your many desires—that eye which rivals a drop of lac transferred to the big toe of Gaurī’s foot when she was appeased by her anger; which possesses the splendor of a ruby set in a crystal stone;
which acts like a tiny fish fallen from the rising celestial river; and which is parched by the fire of liberation.

For the sake of prosperity, may the pair of eyes of the Lord of Śarvāṇī—whose oily hue, proclaiming the destruction of the Daityas, shines clearly as a remnant of a halo around the orbs of the sun and moon;
which, upon my arrival, assumes the state of creation, maintenance, and dissolution while casting away all pride; and which now bestows a playful grace upon your two eyebrows—protect you.
When the pair of eyes was first veiled by the daughter of the Mountain with a garment of darkness-blue cloth, the entire world appeared like a golden lotus turned tawny by the planet Saturn.

May those two eyes of the Lord of the Three Cities—praised as the supreme purifiers for the Leader of the Gods, victorious over the hosts of enemies, and capable of swiftly restraining the horses of your senses—be present here before you.

Thereafter, may the two earrings of the Lord of Caṇḍī—who desires to cast his glance upon them—bring you great prosperity; those earrings which dispel the itching on the cheeks made pale by the white ash of the Blessed One;

which spread a luster with their jeweled tips to soothe that itch; and which, resembling the orb of the fierce sun, are preeminent in shattering the darkness of people who bow perpetually before him, while Indra himself bows down in reverence.

May your nose—possessing the beauty of the pericarp of your lovely lotus-face, with its high, pure, and lofty bridge—be for your eternal protection; it inspires the suspicion of being the great white serpent king hissing as he raises his massive hood, eager to enter the wide-open, gaping cavity of the skull-topped staff (khaṭvāṅga) held by Śiva.

Truly, when the Daughter of the Mountain sees her own form reflected in those two [nostrils] as they exceed [her own] size, she becomes intensely jealous toward her husband, fearing him again and again that he might desire another wife.

May those two cheeks of the Guardian of the World (Indra), which are exceedingly bright like the night of the tenth lunar day and which constantly and loftily desire to see you—the beloved of the celestial river—protect you.

May that lower lip of Viṣṇu grant you prosperity—that lip by whose luster the world-ends are reddened; for the Daughter of the Mountain (Pārvatī), her love intensely aroused, drinks from it with great affection, while the Lord of Beasts (Śiva), desiring to gaze secretly at the Kaustubha gem situated nearby, keeps his poison in his throat out of devotion to his consort.

May that row of teeth grant you long-lasting joy here—teeth which shine exceedingly like a line of foam-drops glistening from the flowing stream of nectar-like, beautiful speech issuing from her moon-like face;
teeth whose lofty tips are purer and brighter than the luster of the moon or the kunda flower, and which surpass the brilliance of the gatekeeper of the sons of Danu.

Deep and having become the Supreme Brahman, it suppresses the roar of the mass of clouds thundering during the rainy season and even the loud sound of the wind standing amidst lightning; [may that voice of hers grant you joy].

May that primordial sound (*sanāda*), which is well-uttered for the manifest-formed Lord of Life whose instruments are revealed, bestow upon you through his true love a state where birth is entirely devoid of fruit.

May the laugh of the eight-formed one (*aṣṭamūrti*) clearly grant you abundant and cherished satisfaction here—his light by which the three worlds shine; who, submerged within the ocean, blows forth with white foam-drops like the spreading expanse of the Ganges’ waters; who is massive in body, terrifying with the roar of "A-ha-hu," and intensely radiant with the luster of his tusks.

The face of Śambhu known as Sadyojāta, which is pure and bestows joy; that called Vāmadeva by name, which resembles gold; the southern face named Aghora, dark like a rain-cloud; that which has the luster of the rising sun and is proclaimed by the Supreme Puruṣa; and the divine one known as Īśāna—may these five faces of Śambhu grant you your heart's desire. (13) Upon her forehead, three lines resembling thick black collyrium shine forth, as if personally fashioned with devotion by Bhavānī herself as a salve for my love.

May the neck of your Lord—whose radiance lasts until the end of the aeon, which is exceedingly beautiful, and whose body is adorned with conch-like lines—shine eternally and intensely within you, O slow-moving one. May the throat of the Enemy of Time (Śiva), which washes away all impurities from the heart, purify your hearts thoroughly—that throat which, while bestowing boons at every step, remained fixed in nectar even as it brought about the death of Kāla; that throat which, seeking a place to rest amidst the splendor of Indra’s tusks and between the great Kaustubha gem on his chest, requested a dwelling from the Mountain Goddess (Pārvatī) who was obstructing its path. 14–15. May that stainless base of the arms of Dhūrjaṭi—which is marked by the impressions of Pārvatī’s beautiful golden bracelets during her firm embraces while agitated by mature love; which is radiant with luster, adorned with dancing serpent-bracelets, and which, having cast away the mental impurities of those who have attained it, destroys all accumulated karma—protect you.
May the streams of the celestial river, as if having reached a neck-embrace from the Lord of the West, appear like long crystal-archways for crossing the ocean of worldly existence.

May those arms of Hara—which serve as the horizontal diameter for the abode of the three worlds, which have torn asunder the bodies of the Daityas like elephants, and which swiftly destroy the multitudes of sins here—protect you.

(17) May that [ash] which was smeared upon the chest of the enemy of Dakṣa—who bowed low under the weight of passion—and which was sprinkled from the beautiful sandalwood paste on Śumbha’s breasts pressed between Pārvatī’s bosoms;

may that ash, which possesses a constant brilliance from the mass of jewels on the hoods of the serpents whose eyes are fixed upon it, and which resembles a slab of crystal, quickly destroy your perpetual sin. (18)

In the vast ocean of milk within the belly of the Enemy of Time (Viṣṇu)—an ocean shimmering with networks of waves filled with various liberated and unliberated beings, possessing a deep whirlpool at the navel, and joined by the swaying of the best of serpents;
in that temple of the Goddess of Splendor, ever-newly radiant and white as the moon’s cool rays—He sports for a long time in His wonderful threefold abode.
Where a tiger skin quivers like a vast, spreading valley within the Himalayas, surrounded on all sides by a mass of dark clouds mingled with thick frost;
where the mountain-born Goddess’s playground has the exceedingly broad girth of the serpent-king as its girdle—may that ample hip of the one whose crest is the young moon lead you to supreme bliss.

May those two [thighs], which serve as the foundation for the firm support of her expansive hips, which are perfectly rounded and constantly uphold the three worlds, and which possess a noble luster like the trunk of Indra’s excellent elephant, [grant you prosperity].

May the two knees of the Destroyer of Cities (Śiva)—which are firm, white as ashes, and which forcibly devour the hosts of enemies—grant you your desires; for they are bowed down deeply by devotees with hearts full of intense devotion.

May those two knees of the Enemy of Death (Śiva), which surpass the moon in luster, grant you beauty; they resemble a casket fashioned from moonstones for the sake of the bliss of the sages, and they perform the rhythmic movements of their dance upon the mirror of the minds of the seers, while the serpent-king’s hood serves as a pillow for them at every moment.

May those two shanks of the Trident-bearer, which shine like great staffs of crystal, bring you grace; they are as white as the moon or a conch shell, and are intensely cherished here in the minds of devotees—shanks that sprout with the luster of priceless gems from the circle of hoods of the preeminent serpent hosts who have become his anklets, and which are praised by the gods of heaven.
They are constantly surrounded by Brahmavid, Devala, and others, who offer abundant services of worship with various hymns and weapons, and who are ever free from all defects.

May those two feet of Śiva— the soles of which possess the beautiful luster of large tortoises— grant you auspiciousness, they who, being perfectly worshipped here in your heart like a lake, eternally proclaim the praises of the Lord;

those toes of the Odd-eyed One, which formerly caused the ten-faced Rāvaṇa to cry out as he shook his own excellent mountain while his mouth bled profusely and his life-force was expelled by the mere falling of a single portion of [Pārvatī’s] body, and which are auspicious, having burnt him to ashes,
and are adorned with clusters of blooming garlands and entwined with the beloved of serpents.

May the row of toenails on the lotus-feet of the Blue-throated Lord (Śiva)—which are incessantly and purely illuminated by the abundant luster of the jewels from the bowstrings and armlets resting upon the shimmering crowns of the foremost gods led by Prācīnabarhis as they bow low; which are exceedingly lofty and appear like a mass of radiant stars bestowed as a gift; and which grant happiness—may that row bestow bliss upon you.

And may those two [feet], which attain a blossoming even when the moon-like face of Satyabhāmā approaches them, and which, like a lake, confer beauty upon every heart here while bestowing it upon the gods... [27]

May those lotus-feet of the Lord who holds the deer-marked moon in his hand—feet which possess a most stainless luster and which wise men ever serve, just as a swarm of bees serves a cluster of blossoming lotuses—bring you prosperity.

May the pollen from the lotus-feet of Śrīkaṇṭha, rising from his feet that glow with a dawn-like radiance, long bring about the destruction of your sins; for by the grace of those feet alone, ascetics whose forms are bowed in devotion proceed to liberation, their very selves becoming like the serpent Śeṣa upon the heads of the assembly of gods in heaven.

May that splendor of Maheśa—which, by its abundance, has pervaded the world; which is the supreme abode of all luminous things; which is the essential truth of the Sāmans as taught in the Vedas; which is the primordial state beyond all qualities; and which the great ones repeatedly and loudly call "Aho," "motionless," and "profound"—may that worshipful light destroy my daily delusion. Thus ends [the work] of the venerable Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka Ācārya.
In the work of the venerable Śaṅkara Bhagavat, disciple of the venerable Govinda Bhagavatpūjyapāda,
the hymn of praise describing [the Lord] from the hair on His head down to His feet is complete.
